passage: Thursday. Harish's diary. Before the Hindi test, Vishal sat at his desk twisting his hands round and round, like he was wringing out a wet towel. I thought, He's scared of the test, like me. So I leaned over and said, “Want to go over the matras? I keep mixing them up too.” He shook his head. Then he said, really quietly, “My Dadi went to hospital last night.” I didn't know what to say, so I just sat closer till the bell. I told Ma'am at break, and she let Vishal phone home at lunch. So it wasn't the test at all.

qa.q: Where did Vishal's Dadi go last night?
qa.a: Vishal's Dadi went to hospital last night.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling as he wrung his hands?
qa.a: He was worried and frightened about his Dadi in hospital; Harish first guessed test nerves, which shows the hands alone didn't reveal the cause.

qa.q: Which of Harish's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Offering a friendly word opened the door, and telling Ma'am meant Vishal got to phone home at lunch.

qa.q: How did Harish first read the wringing hands?
qa.a: Harish assumed it was test nerves, because that's what Harish felt too, before hearing the real reason.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hand-wringing as test nerves, offering a friendly word, and finding a different cause.

passage: The oral test was the first thing that winter morning at the village school, and the inspector's jeep was already outside. Yusuf sat on the bench wringing his hands, squeezing and twisting his fingers over and over. Zubin watched. He's terrified. Zubin slid along the bench. “You know the tables better than anyone. You taught me seven.” Yusuf blew on his fingers and gave a small smile. “Thanks. I am scared. But I also did the milking at five, and my hands are frozen stiff.” Zubin laughed and rubbed his own cold hands. “Then let's warm them up together.”

qa.q: When did Yusuf do the milking?
qa.a: Yusuf did the milking at five.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling as he wrung his hands?
qa.a: Yusuf was scared of the oral test, as he admitted, but his hands were also frozen stiff from the early milking.

qa.q: Why was Zubin's friendly word a good choice?
qa.a: It reminded Yusuf of his real skill and showed support, whatever the cause of the hand-wringing.

qa.q: How did Zubin first read Yusuf's hands?
qa.a: Zubin thought Yusuf was terrified, which was partly right, but the cold was another reason he hadn't guessed.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hand-wringing as nerves, offering a kind word, and finding cold was part of it too.

passage: Before the spelling test in their Dublin classroom, Clara noticed Liam at the next desk rubbing and twisting his hands together, round and round, head down. Poor Liam, she thought. He always panics. She tore a corner off her page, wrote You'll be grand! with a smiley face, and slid it over. Liam read it, then held up his hands. They were shiny. “Sanitiser,” he whispered. “Too much. It won't dry.” Clara snorted. Then he added, “But thanks. I am a bit nervous about ‘necessary’.” She wrote on the corner: one collar, two sleeves. He grinned.

qa.q: What was on Liam's hands?
qa.a: Liam had too much sanitiser on his hands.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling before the test?
qa.a: Liam was a bit nervous about spelling “necessary”, though the hand-twisting was mostly from sanitiser that wouldn't dry.

qa.q: What made Clara's note a good choice even though she guessed wrong?
qa.a: A friendly word helps whatever the cause, and it led Liam to share his real worry, so Clara could help with the spelling 🙂

qa.q: How did Clara read Liam's twisting hands?
qa.a: Clara thought he was panicking as usual, not realising sanitiser explained most of it.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hand-twisting as worry, a friendly word helping, and the signal alone not proving the cause.

passage: I'm Gurleen, and last summer I visited my cousin Uday in London. At the bus stop, a lady offered to take our photo, and I did a V-sign like I always do in pictures, but with the back of my hand facing her. Her smile went stiff. Uday grabbed my wrist and turned it round. “Not that way here!” he whispered. Later he explained that backwards, with the palm facing you, it's a rude sign in Britain. My face burned; I'd done it in every photo since Delhi. Now, before a trip, I ask someone what the hand signs mean there.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen visit Uday?
qa.a: Gurleen visited Uday in London.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel after Uday explained the sign?
qa.a: Gurleen felt embarrassed, face burning, realising the backward V had been in every photo since Delhi.

qa.q: What habit did Gurleen take up, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Asking what hand signs mean before a trip, because the same gesture can be friendly at home and rude elsewhere.

qa.q: What might the lady at the bus stop have thought?
qa.a: She might have felt insulted for a moment, not knowing Gurleen meant it as a friendly photo pose.

grounding: Shows a child learning that a V-sign friendly at home is rude backwards in Britain, and that care with gestures when travelling is wise.

passage: Teacher's note, Wednesday. Aparna, Class 5. Rehana joined us last month after four years in São Paulo, where her father worked. Today I made the OK sign, thumb and finger in a circle, to praise her map. Her face fell, and she hid the map under her book. At break I asked her what happened. She said, very softly, that in Brazil that sign is rude, and children there used it as an insult. I apologised and explained that here it means “perfect”. We agreed I'd use a thumbs-up or just say “well done” with her. Tomorrow I'll ask the class to share gestures from places they've lived.

qa.q: Where had Rehana lived for four years?
qa.a: Rehana had lived in São Paulo for four years.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she hid her map?
qa.a: Rehana felt hurt and confused, reading the OK sign as the insult it was in Brazil rather than as praise.

qa.q: What did Aparna do that repaired things?
qa.a: She asked privately, apologised, explained the local meaning and agreed on a thumbs-up or words instead.

qa.q: What would change if Aparna had not asked at break?
qa.a: Rehana might have believed her teacher was insulting her and felt unwelcome in the new class.

grounding: Shows an OK sign meaning praise in one place and an insult in another, and care with gestures around new friends.

passage: Sunday night. Bidisha's diary. Vandana Didi wrote me a long message about her first week at college in Pune, and I was eating, so I just sent 👍. An hour later Mumma said Didi had called her, upset, asking if I was angry with her. ANGRY? For me 👍 means “great, love it!” Mumma said that for some people, especially grown-ups, a thumbs-up on its own can feel like “okay, whatever, stop talking.” I felt terrible. I called Didi, told her I'd read every word and asked about her hostel roommate. She laughed and said, “Next time send a sentence, Bidi!”

qa.q: Where did Vandana Didi start college?
qa.a: Vandana Didi started college in Pune.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling on hearing Didi was upset?
qa.a: Bidisha felt shocked and then terrible, because the thumbs-up was meant as warm approval, not anger.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do to repair it?
qa.a: Bidisha called Didi, said every word had been read and asked about the roommate, showing real interest.

qa.q: Why might Vandana Didi read a lone thumbs-up as cold?
qa.a: After a long, personal message, a single thumbs-up can feel like a brush-off, especially to someone who uses it that way.

grounding: Shows a thumbs-up meaning warm approval to one person and a cold brush-off to another, and care with new or different readers.

passage: Note for staff, Teachers' Day. Kishore, Class 4. During the celebration, many children bent to touch my feet, as their families do with elders. It is a lovely custom. Kashish stood at the back, twisting her dupatta. A colleague nudged her forward: “Go on, touch Sir's feet.” Kashish's face tightened, and she stepped back. I said, “A namaste means just as much to me, Kashish.” She pressed her palms together and smiled properly for the first time that day. A reminder to all of us: children show respect in many ways, and no child should be pushed into touching anyone.

qa.q: What did Kashish twist while standing at the back?
qa.a: Kashish twisted her dupatta.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she was nudged forward?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable and reluctant, shown by her tightened face and stepping back; she may also simply have felt shy in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did Kishore respect Kashish's choice?
qa.a: Kishore offered a namaste as an equally good way to show respect, so Kashish didn't have to touch anyone.

qa.q: How might the colleague who nudged her see the custom?
qa.a: The colleague probably saw touching feet as the proper way to show respect and didn't notice Kashish's discomfort.

grounding: Shows touching elders' feet as a respectful tradition, other ways of showing respect, and no child being pushed into unwanted touch.

passage: Saturday. Harsha's diary. Today was Leela Paati's eightieth birthday. When we reached her house, I bent down and touched her feet, like Amma taught me, and she put her hand on my head and said, “Nalla iru, kanna,” which means be well. Her hand was soft and shaky. I felt warm all over, like a blanket. My cousin Pranav, who lives in America, stood behind me looking confused. Later he asked me why. I said it's how we show respect and get blessings, but Paati is happy with a namaste too. He did a namaste, and Paati laughed and hugged him anyway.

qa.q: What did Leela Paati say to Harsha?
qa.a: She said, “Nalla iru, kanna,” which means be well.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel after Paati's blessing?
qa.a: Harsha felt warm and loved, like a blanket, from the touch of her soft hand.

qa.q: Which part of Harsha's explanation helped Pranav most?
qa.a: Saying that Paati is happy with a namaste too gave Pranav a comfortable way to show respect without copying a custom he didn't know.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav felt confused at first, then included when his namaste was welcomed with a laugh and a hug 😊

grounding: Shows a child touching an elder's feet to show respect and receive a blessing, and that respect can be shown in other ways too.

passage: At the wedding in their village near Jodhpur, the courtyard was full of relatives Preeti had never met. Her mother led her from elder to elder. Preeti bent and touched each pair of feet, quick and neat, and got pats on the head. Then a tall man with a big moustache, Lokesh-ji, a distant uncle, laughed and grabbed her wrist. “Come, come, touch properly, and give me a hug too.” Preeti's body went stiff, and she pulled back. Her mother stepped between them at once. “She has greeted you with respect, Lokesh-ji. A namaste is enough.” She kept Preeti beside her all evening and later told her, “You were right to pull back.”

qa.q: What did Lokesh-ji ask Preeti to give him besides touching his feet?
qa.a: He asked her to give him a hug too.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when her body went stiff?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and uneasy at being grabbed and asked for a hug by a man she didn't know.

qa.q: How did Preeti's mother protect her?
qa.a: She stepped between them at once, said a namaste was enough, kept Preeti beside her and told her she was right to pull back.

qa.q: How might the relatives nearby see her mother's words?
qa.a: Some might think she was being strict, but others would see a mother making sure respect never means unwanted touch.

grounding: Shows a child touching elders' feet as respect, and an adult making sure she is never forced into unwelcome touch.

passage: Monday. Zeenat's diary. On the school bus I was telling Nikita about the puppy Abbu might bring home, and I got louder and louder. Nikita pressed both palms down in the air, slowly, like she was pushing a lid closed. I stopped. It felt like, Shut up, nobody cares. I turned to the window and sulked. Then I noticed her face: eyebrows up, eyes flicking to the front. The conductor was glaring at the back rows and had already told two boys off. Nikita whispered, “Sorry! I want to hear. Just quieter, or he'll shout.” So I whispered the rest. She squeezed my hand at the puppy's name.

qa.q: Who was glaring at the back rows?
qa.a: The conductor was glaring at the back rows.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Nikita pressed her palms down?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and dismissed, reading it as “shut up, nobody cares”.

qa.q: What cues helped Zeenat read the gesture differently?
qa.a: Nikita's raised eyebrows, eyes flicking to the front and whispered sorry showed worry about the conductor, not boredom.

qa.q: What was Nikita trying to say with the gesture?
qa.a: Nikita wanted to keep hearing the story and was worried the conductor would shout at them.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's palms-down gesture as dismissive, then using face and tone to see it was worry.

passage: The whole class was shouting about the kite festival on the temple ground, and Karthik was loudest. “Mine will go higher than the water tank!” Pallavi Teacher stood at the front and pressed both palms slowly downwards, twice. Karthik stopped. Is she cross? He checked her face. She was smiling, eyebrows relaxed, and her voice when it came was soft: “Lower, lower. I want to hear about the kites, not the whole village.” The class giggled and dropped to a murmur. Karthik raised his hand and said, in a normal voice, “Teacher, mine has a tail made from my Paati's old sari.” “Then it will fly beautifully,” she said.

qa.q: What is Karthik's kite tail made from?
qa.a: Karthik's kite tail is made from his Paati's old sari.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when Pallavi Teacher pressed her palms down?
qa.a: He felt a flash of worry that she was cross, until her smile and soft voice showed otherwise.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi Teacher's gesture work without upsetting anyone?
qa.a: The palms-down meant lower your voice, and pairing it with a smile, relaxed eyebrows and a soft joke made it kind, not dismissive.

qa.q: What would change if Pallavi had made the same gesture with a frown and a sharp voice?
qa.a: The class might have felt scolded and gone silent, and Karthik might not have shared his kite story.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's slow-down gesture as lower your voice, with face and tone showing it was kind.

passage: In the school library in Toronto, Wei rushed over to Daniel, words tumbling out. “I got into the robotics team! They picked six from the whole grade!” Daniel, typing at the library computer, didn't turn round. He pressed one palm down twice in the air, eyes on the screen. “Calm down, it's just a club.” Wei's grin faded. The same gesture his coach used to settle the team before a match felt totally different now: no smile, no eye contact, a flat voice. Wei walked off. At lunch Daniel came over, red-faced. “Sorry about earlier. I was upset I didn't get picked. Congrats, really.”

qa.q: How many students did the robotics team pick?
qa.a: They picked six from the whole grade.

qa.q: What was Wei feeling when his grin faded?
qa.a: Wei felt hurt and brushed off, because the palm-down came with no smile, no eye contact and a flat voice.

qa.q: What did Daniel do later that helped?
qa.a: Daniel apologised, explained he was upset about not being picked and gave real congratulations.

qa.q: What was behind Daniel's gesture?
qa.a: Daniel was disappointed about not making the team himself, and it came out as a dismissive calm down.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's slow-down gesture as dismissive because of the face and tone that came with it.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: The gilli-danda game behind the village temple had turned into shouting. “You're out!” “I'm not! It didn't touch the ground!” Nazia and two boys were nose to nose. Chaitanya, holding the danda, stepped into the middle and made a T with his hands, high above his head. “Time out! Time out!” Everyone stopped, panting. “We're fighting about the rule, not the game,” he said. “Let's ask Rafi Chacha. He's played for forty years.” They trooped to the tea stall. Rafi Chacha said the gilli has to touch the ground first. Nazia was not out. Chaitanya made the T again, then turned it into a thumbs-up. “Game on.”

qa.q: Who did they ask about the rule?
qa.a: They asked Rafi Chacha at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he stepped into the middle?
qa.a: He was probably worried the shouting would turn into a real fight and wanted to calm everyone down.

qa.q: Why did the time-out work here?
qa.a: It paused the quarrel to clarify the rule with someone fair, so the game could restart without bad feelings.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel after the rule was checked?
qa.a: Nazia probably felt relieved and fairly treated, since the rule showed she was not out.

grounding: Shows a child using the time-out T honestly to pause a quarrel and clarify a rule, lowering conflict.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: Liam was losing at tag in the Auckland park, and he knew it. Wei was two steps behind him when Liam spun round and made a T with his hands. “Time out! Shoelace!” Wei stopped. Liam bent over his shoe, which was already tied, and caught his breath. Then he ran off again, laughing. Ten minutes later, cornered by the slide, he made the T again. “Time out! Stitch!” Wei folded his arms. “That's your second time out, and both times I nearly had you.” The others had noticed too. Liam's face went pink. “Okay,” he muttered. “No more. You got me.” He held out his arm for Wei to tag.

qa.q: Where did Wei corner Liam?
qa.a: Wei cornered Liam by the slide.

qa.q: What was Liam likely feeling when he made the T the second time?
qa.a: He was probably tired and embarrassed about losing, using the time-out to avoid being caught rather than for a real need.

qa.q: What made Wei's response fair?
qa.a: Wei calmly pointed out the pattern instead of shouting, which let Liam admit it and play on honestly.

qa.q: How did the other children see Liam's time-outs?
qa.a: They noticed too, so the dodge made Liam look less fair in the game.

grounding: Shows a child using the time-out gesture to dodge losing, and peers spotting it.

subtype: Time-out gesture and pausing a game [Expressing]
passage: In the practice match at the district football academy, Nilesh and a defender clashed heads going for the ball. Nilesh sat down hard and didn't get up. Play went on around him. Varun, his teammate, stopped dead, turned towards the coach's bench and made a big T with both hands. “Time out! Nilesh is hurt!” The coach blew the whistle at once and jogged over. Nilesh was holding his forehead, dazed. The coach knelt, checked his eyes, asked him a few questions, then sent him to the medical room with the assistant. Afterwards the coach found Varun. “Good call. That's exactly what the T is for.”

qa.q: Where did the coach send Nilesh?
qa.a: The coach sent Nilesh to the medical room with the assistant.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he stopped dead?
qa.a: Varun was worried and alarmed that Nilesh was hurt and that nobody had noticed.

qa.q: Why was Varun's time-out an honest use of the signal?
qa.a: It paused the game to get help for a real injury, which is exactly what the T is meant for.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt sitting dazed while play went on?
qa.a: Nilesh may have felt confused and alone until Varun's signal brought the coach over.

grounding: Shows a child using the time-out T to pause a game and get help, an honest use that keeps players safe.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: In the science lab, Rukmini Ma'am was explaining how a ball rolls down a ramp. Her right hand swooped down steeply, then shot along the bench. “It speeds up like this!” Tanvir watched her hand. So it goes really fast at the bottom, faster than a cycle? When they tried it, the marble trundled down and rolled gently off the end. Tanvir frowned and raised his hand. “Ma'am, your hand went way faster than the marble. Which is right?” Ma'am laughed. “Good catch. My hands exaggerate. It does speed up, but only a little on a ramp this small. Let's time it and see.”

qa.q: What did the marble do at the end of the ramp?
qa.a: The marble rolled gently off the end.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when the marble rolled gently?
qa.a: Tanvir felt puzzled, because the gesture had made him expect something much faster.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir's follow-up question useful?
qa.a: It checked the gesture against what he saw, and led Ma'am to admit her hands exaggerated and to time it properly.

qa.q: How did Rukmini Ma'am react to being corrected?
qa.a: She laughed, called it a good catch and turned it into a timing test, so she was glad he asked.

grounding: Shows a pupil reading a teacher's gestures for speed in a demo, noticing they exaggerated, and asking to check.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Gurleen, and Deepika sits in front of me in geography. Sir was describing how the river flows from the mountains. He held his left hand high for the mountain, then waved his right hand down and away to his right. Deepika drew the path in her notebook, arrow going right. But on the wall map the river flows left, towards the sea. Sir was facing us, so his right was our left. Deepika looked from her notebook to the map and back, frowning. Then she put her hand up. “Sir, is it flowing left or right?” He looked at his own hand and laughed. “Left, from where you sit. My hands were backwards for you.”

qa.q: Which way does the river flow on the wall map?
qa.a: On the wall map the river flows left, towards the sea.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she looked from her notebook to the map?
qa.a: She was confused and a little unsure, because the gesture and the map didn't match.

qa.q: What did Deepika's question achieve?
qa.a: It showed the teacher's gesture was mirrored from the class's side, so everyone could correct their arrows.

qa.q: How did Gurleen make sense of the mix-up?
qa.a: Gurleen worked out that Sir was facing the class, so his right was their left.

grounding: Shows a pupil following a teacher's direction gestures, being misled by a mirrored picture, and asking to check the meaning.

subtype: Reading a speaker's gestures for meaning [Interpreting]
passage: Tuesday: Suraj Bhaiya was teaching Sunaina to bowl in the lane. “Land it here,” he said, and his hand dipped to the ground, then bounced up to his knee. Sunaina bowled. The ball smacked into the ground halfway and bounced over his head. Thursday: She tried again, watching his hands closely. His hand bounced to his knee again, but he was crouching this time, so his knee was lower. She bowled even shorter. Saturday: Before bowling, Sunaina asked, “Bhaiya, show me with something real where it lands. Your hands keep changing.” He drew a chalk mark on the lane. Her next ball hit it.

qa.q: What did Suraj draw on the lane on Saturday?
qa.a: He drew a chalk mark on the lane.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling by Saturday?
qa.a: Sunaina was frustrated and confused by the changing hand signs, and determined to get a clearer answer.

qa.q: Why did asking for a real mark work better?
qa.a: A chalk mark showed exactly where to land the ball, while his hand gestures kept changing and misled her.

qa.q: How might Suraj see his hand gestures after Saturday?
qa.a: Suraj might realise his gestures weren't as clear as he thought, and that a real mark helps more.

grounding: Shows a child reading a speaker's hand gestures for height and distance, being misled, and asking a follow-up to check.

passage: I'm Mehak. When Gargi, the new girl, asked how to get to my house for the project, words just weren't working. “Past the temple, then… no, before the temple…” So I drew it in the air with my finger: a straight line for the main road, a loop round the park, a sharp left at the chemist. Halfway through, my finger stopped. “Wait. If you cut through the park here,” I jabbed at the air, “you skip the whole loop.” I'd never noticed that, even though I walk it every day. Gargi copied the shape in the air with her own finger and nodded. She got there in ten minutes.

qa.q: Where is the sharp left in Mehak's directions?
qa.a: The sharp left is at the chemist.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when the finger stopped halfway?
qa.a: Mehak felt surprised and pleased at discovering a shortcut through the park while tracing the route.

qa.q: Why did tracing in the air work better than words?
qa.a: It let Mehak show the shape of the route and think it through, finding a shortcut that words had missed.

qa.q: How might Gargi, new to the area, have found the air map?
qa.a: Gargi could copy the shape with her own finger, which made the route easier to picture and remember.

grounding: Shows a child tracing a map in the air to explain the way home, and the gesture helping the child work out a new idea.

passage: Class note, Monday. Devika, science. In today's oral quiz I asked Bidisha how a thrown ball moves. She started, “It goes up and then…” and stopped, hands clamped under her desk. Last term another teacher told her to keep her hands still when answering. I said, “Use your hands if it helps.” Her finger shot up and drew a smooth arch in the air: rising, slowing at the top, then curving down faster. “Up slow, then down fast. Like a rainbow, but lopsided because of the wind.” That was a better answer than most of my older classes give. Note to self: let children gesture while they explain.

qa.q: What shape did Bidisha draw in the air?
qa.a: Bidisha drew a smooth arch in the air.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha stop and clamp her hands under her desk?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about being told off, since another teacher had told her to keep her hands still, and without them she felt stuck.

qa.q: What did Devika do that helped Bidisha explain?
qa.a: Devika told her to use her hands if it helped, which let Bidisha show and work out the ball's path.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had kept the no-hands rule?
qa.a: Bidisha might have stayed stuck, and Devika would never have heard how well she understood the ball's path.

grounding: Shows a child tracing a ball's route in the air to explain it, and how letting children gesture aids explanation.

passage: Wednesday. Aadhya's diary. Today at break Payal didn't get how I'd scored in the carrom game yesterday. I tried saying it: “The striker hit the side, then came back and knocked the red in.” She looked blank. So I traced it in the air, again and again: my finger shot to the edge, bounced off at an angle and zigzagged back to the corner. While I was drawing it, I suddenly understood why it worked: the angle in was the same as the angle out! Payal copied the zigzag with her finger and said, “Oh! Like a ball off a wall.” Tomorrow I'm going to try it on purpose.

qa.q: What did Aadhya's striker knock in?
qa.a: The striker knocked the red in.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling while tracing the shot?
qa.a: Aadhya felt excited and surprised, suddenly understanding that the angle in matched the angle out.

qa.q: Why is it worth letting children gesture when explaining?
qa.a: Tracing helped Aadhya explain the shot to Payal and also work out the idea, which words alone had not done.

qa.q: How did Payal understand the shot in the end?
qa.a: Payal copied the zigzag with her own finger and linked it to a ball bouncing off a wall.

grounding: Shows a child tracing a path in the air to explain a shot, and the gesture helping the child work out the idea.

passage: “Why did you jump up like that?” Usha giggled as her grandmother shuffled into the room with a plate of banana chips. Indu sat back down, cheeks warm. “At my house we always stand when an elder comes in. My Nanaji says it's respect.” “We don't. Ammachi would say sit, sit, don't make a fuss.” Ammachi set the plate down and patted Indu's shoulder. “Such good manners. In my father's house we stood too. Now my knees are old, so everyone sits!” Usha stopped giggling. “So it's not weird?” “Different houses, different ways,” said Ammachi. “Both are respect.” Indu grinned and took a chip.

qa.q: What did Ammachi bring in?
qa.a: Ammachi brought a plate of banana chips.

qa.q: Why were Indu's cheeks warm after sitting back down?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed when Usha giggled, worried the habit of standing looked strange in this house.

qa.q: How did Ammachi help both children?
qa.a: She praised Indu's manners, shared that her own family once stood too and said both ways are respect, so no one felt wrong.

qa.q: How might Usha feel after Ammachi's words?
qa.a: Usha probably felt a little sheepish and more understanding, seeing that standing up was a family custom, not something weird.

grounding: Shows a child standing when an elder enters as respect, and how such rules differ between families.

passage: I'm Harsha, and when I started karate last year, the first thing Nirmala Sensei taught us wasn't a kick. It was the bow: feet together, hands at our sides, bend from the waist before stepping on the mat, and kneel in a line at the end. The first time, I felt silly. When I showed my friends at school, Kunal laughed. “You bow to her? That's so weak.” I didn't know what to say. At the next class I asked Sensei. She said, “We bow to say thank you for the teaching, and to the mat for keeping us safe. Strong people show respect.” Now I bow without feeling silly at all.

qa.q: What did Nirmala Sensei teach first?
qa.a: She taught the bow first, not a kick.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel the first time bowing?
qa.a: Harsha felt silly and self-conscious, and later unsure what to say when Kunal called it weak.

qa.q: What did Harsha do after being teased, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Harsha asked Sensei what the bow meant, which gave a real reason to feel proud instead of silly.

qa.q: Why might Kunal see bowing as weak?
qa.a: Kunal may not know that in karate the bow means thanks and respect, so he read it as giving in.

grounding: Shows a child learning to bow and kneel in a karate class as respect, not weakness, with rules differing between settings.

passage: Class note, Friday. Jaya, Grade 5. Kashish joined us from a school in Varanasi this week. Every time a teacher enters, she stands up straight beside her desk, as her old school taught. Nobody else here does. Today two boys started standing up and sitting down to mock her, and Kashish went scarlet and stayed seated all afternoon, eyes down. At the end of the day I spoke to the class: “In many schools and homes, standing when an elder enters is respect. Here we don't need to, but it's never wrong.” I told Kashish privately she can stand or sit, whichever feels right. I spoke to the two boys before they left.

qa.q: Where did Kashish come from?
qa.a: Kashish came from a school in Varanasi.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she stayed seated all afternoon?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed after being mocked for standing, so she hid a habit she had been proud of.

qa.q: How did Jaya respect both sets of school rules?
qa.a: Jaya explained to the class that standing is respect elsewhere, told Kashish privately she could choose, and dealt with the mocking boys the same day.

qa.q: How might the two boys see standing up after Jaya spoke?
qa.a: They might realise it was a sign of respect from another school, not something odd to mock.

grounding: Shows a child standing when teachers enter as respect, and how such rules differ across schools.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: In the evening study hall at the boarding school, Kunal sat sprawled low in his chair, feet stretched out, chin almost on his chest, a physics book propped on his stomach. Lokesh Sir stopped beside him. “Kunal. Sit up. If you're bored, go to bed.” Kunal pushed himself upright. “I'm not bored, Sir. I'm on the magnets chapter. I think better leaning back.” Sir raised an eyebrow. “Tell me why a magnet sticks to the steel cupboard but not the wooden door.” Kunal answered, clearly. Sir nodded slowly. “All right. Lean back here. In class, though, other teachers will read it as not caring.” Kunal hadn't known that.

qa.q: Which chapter was Kunal reading?
qa.a: Kunal was on the magnets chapter.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Sir asked if he was bored?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and a bit defensive, since he was concentrating and hadn't realised his slouch looked like boredom.

qa.q: How did Lokesh Sir check his first reading?
qa.a: He asked a question about the chapter, and Kunal's clear answer showed the slouch wasn't boredom.

qa.q: How do teachers often read a slouch like Kunal's?
qa.a: Many teachers read it as not caring or boredom, even when a student is actually thinking comfortably.

grounding: Shows a child learning that teachers read slouching as boredom, when it was a comfortable way of thinking.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Lalit, and I sit across the aisle from Nandini. This week she's been slumped over her desk every morning, shoulders rounded, head on her arm. On Wednesday Ma'am snapped, “Nandini, sit up, this is not a bedroom!” Nandini sat up, but a minute later she'd sunk down again. She's usually the first with her hand up. I don't know what's going on with her. But she also hasn't eaten her tiffin all week, and she doesn't laugh at Kiran's jokes anymore. At break I told Ma'am. Ma'am's face changed. She took Nandini for a walk round the garden, just the two of them, and later that day she called Nandini's mother.

qa.q: What has Nandini not eaten all week?
qa.a: Nandini hasn't eaten her tiffin all week.

qa.q: What might Nandini be feeling behind her slump?
qa.a: She might be tired or low and sad about something, since she has stopped eating and laughing; boredom seems less likely for someone usually first with her hand up.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that helped?
qa.a: Lalit told Ma'am about the other signs, which helped her see the slump as a clue to low mood and check in privately.

qa.q: How did Ma'am first read Nandini's posture?
qa.a: Ma'am first read it as laziness or boredom and told her to sit up, until Lalit's details changed her view.

grounding: Shows slouching read by a teacher as boredom when it may signal tiredness or low mood, and posture being a clue, not proof.

subtype: Slouching and sitting up in class [Interpreting]
passage: Monday: In the first week of Ramzan, Asif sat slumped in the back row by afternoon, chin on his fist. Pema, beside him, thought he'd stopped caring about the science project they were doing together. She did the diagram alone, annoyed. Wednesday: At lunch Pema found Asif in the library instead of the canteen, head resting on a book. “Aren't you eating?” “I'm fasting till sunset. I get really tired after three.” Pema felt her face go hot. Friday: Pema moved their project work to the first period, when Asif sat up straight and full of ideas. By afternoon he could slouch, and she didn't mind.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: I'm Deepak. Last year, my leg never stopped bouncing in tuition. Nilesh Sir would say, “Deepak, still!” and I'd freeze it, and then my whole brain went into keeping the leg still instead of the sums. One evening before the unit test, I was pacing the corridor, round and round, and Sir came out. I thought I was in trouble. Instead he said, “Is it nerves or energy?” I said, “Both, I think.” He said, “Then walk to the gate and back, twice, and come in.” I did, and sat down calmer. After that he gave the whole group a stretch break every twenty minutes. My sums got better.

qa.q: How often did Sir give the group a stretch break?
qa.a: Sir gave the group a stretch break every twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling while pacing before the test?
qa.a: Deepak was nervous and full of energy, and at first worried about being in trouble when Sir came out.

qa.q: Why did the stretch breaks help?
qa.a: They let Deepak use up energy instead of spending effort keeping still, which helped with focus on the sums.

qa.q: How did Nilesh Sir first see the bouncing leg?
qa.a: Nilesh Sir first saw it as something to stop, not realising keeping still took all Deepak's attention.

grounding: Shows a child pacing and bouncing a leg from nerves and energy, and movement breaks helping focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: Class note, Tuesday. Sunaina, Class 3. Thomas's file from last year says “defiant, won't stay seated.” After two weeks, I don't see defiance. I see a boy who is up and down, jiggling and drumming, especially after long sitting or before tests, but who says sorry and sits again when I ask. So this week I gave him jobs: carrying the register, cleaning the board, handing out copies. After each errand he sits and works for a good stretch. Today, before the spelling test, he paced by the window for a minute, then sat down and got his best score yet. I've told his parents we'll keep the movement breaks.

qa.q: What did Thomas's file from last year say?
qa.a: It said “defiant, won't stay seated.”

qa.q: What might Thomas be feeling when he paces before a test?
qa.a: He is probably nervous or restless with energy, and moving helps him settle rather than being a sign of defiance.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina's errands work?
qa.a: They gave Thomas a regular chance to move, so he could sit and work for a good stretch afterwards.

qa.q: How did last year's teacher read Thomas's movement?
qa.a: Last year's teacher read it as defiance, perhaps without trying movement breaks to see if they helped.

grounding: Shows an energetic child who fidgets and paces being misread as defiant, and movement breaks helping focus.

subtype: Pacing and fidgeting for energy or worry [Expressing]
passage: Saturday. Lakshmi's diary. The recital was at six. From four o'clock I couldn't sit. I walked from my room to the kitchen to the balcony and back, again and again, and when Amma made me sit to eat, my leg bounced so hard the plate rattled. Siddharth said, “Relax, why are you so scared?” But I wasn't scared, not mostly. It felt like fizzy water inside me, like I had to move or I'd pop. Amma said, “Go dance through your piece in the hall once.” I did it twice, and afterwards I could eat. On stage I didn't miss a single step. I'm still fizzy now.

qa.q: What time was the recital?
qa.a: The recital was at six.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling while pacing before the recital?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt mostly excited, fizzy inside with energy, rather than scared as Siddharth thought.

qa.q: Why was Amma's idea helpful?
qa.a: Dancing through the piece used up the energy, so Lakshmi could eat and feel ready.

qa.q: How did Siddharth read the pacing?
qa.a: Siddharth read it as fear, missing that it was mostly excitement and a need to move.

grounding: Shows a child pacing and bouncing a leg from excitement rather than fear, and movement helping them settle.
